articles.excerpt: Psychic spies shouldn’t be this boring
articles.body: AMC brought its adaptation of Anne Rice’s Interview with the Vampire to Netflix in 2024, kicking off a deal to give the streaming service access to its interconnected Immortal Universe. The phenomenal show recently completed its third season – renamed The Vampire Lestat – and has been renewed for a fourth season. Netflix is also the home to the first two seasons of Mayfair Witches , a series about a neurosurgeon who discovers she’s part of an ancient line of witches. While Interview with the Vampire skillfully navigates time jumps across centuries, Mayfair Witches buckles under the weight of its generational tale. But its sexy story still landed it a third season, expected to release next year.

articles.body: There are still a few years left in the 2020s, but it’s already been a fantastic decade for science fiction movies . The Dune films are likely the biggest highlight, as director Denis Villeneuve has finally brought the proper scale to Frank Herbert’s novels from the 1960s. The 2010s were certainly a better decade for the superhero sub-genre of sci-fi than the 2020s have been, particularly for Marvel Studios, but there have still been some breakout comic book films like Deadpool & Wolverine , Superman , and a trio of Spider-Man films. Even some non-franchise sci-fi films have managed to achieve greatness, like Project Hail Mary .

This post walks through exactly how to do that — commands, policies, validation steps, and the reasoning behind each decision. articles.title: Backpropagation by Hand: Two Layers, a Pen, and Then Autograd Agrees
articles.excerpt: in the last piece i did autograd, and the whole point of it was that you call loss.backward() once and pytorch fills in every gradient for you, and a couple of people basically said the same thing bac…
articles.body: in the last piece i did autograd, and the whole point of it was that you call loss.backward() once and pytorch fills in every gradient for you, and a couple of people basically said the same thing back to me, ok that is nice but on a real network with more than one layer what is it actually doing in there. so this time i want to do the thing you will genuinely never do inside a training loop, i want to take a two-layer network and compute every gradient by hand, one node at a time, and then type the same thing into pytorch and watch autograd land on the exact same numbers. the one-neuron version was the warm-up. this is the one where the chain rule has to travel back through a hidden layer, and where the interesting failures live. The network, small enough to hold in your head Two layers.

articles.title: What 166K Clicks Taught Me About Using AI for SEO
articles.excerpt: Over three months, my static website generated 166K Google clicks from 1.39M impressions, with an 11.9% CTR and 7.5 average position. The graph also shows traffic declining after its peak. That is imp…
articles.body: Over three months, my static website generated 166K Google clicks from 1.39M impressions , with an 11.9% CTR and 7.5 average position . The graph also shows traffic declining after its peak. That is important: AI did not create automatic, permanent growth. What helped was using AI inside a measurable SEO workflow—and reverting ideas when the data disagreed. Here is the loop I now use. 1. Use Keyword Planner for discovery, not decisions I start with broad product terms in Google Keyword Planner and export the results. Search volume and competition help me find possible clusters, but a high-volume keyword is not automatically a reason to create a page. Before choosing one, I ask: Does it match my product? Is its intent different from pages I already have?

articles.excerpt: Acclaimed literary critic and Senior Editor at The Atlantic Adam Kirsch explores humanity's insatiable drive to wonder at unidentified phenomena in the skies.
articles.body: After all these years, we still want to believe. Whether you're a bona fide believer or a staunch skeptic, we can all agree that UFO legends and lore is a fascinating subject that continues to fuel endless debate. And with pop culture feeding our lizard brains lurid tales of flying saucers and alien invasions , it’s no wonder humanity is always up for a good story of inexplicable aerial sightings or various uncanny encounters of the third kind. In " We Want To Believe: How Aliens Went Mainstream And Why It Matters " (Aug. 25, Columbia Global Reports), acclaimed literary critic and Senior Editor at The Atlantic Adam Kirsch explores this insatiable drive to wonder at unidentified phenomena. For Kirsch, the topic asks many of the same questions that human religions do.

articles.title: On this day in space! Aug. 22, 1963: X-15 sets world altitude record
articles.excerpt: On this day in space! Aug. 22, 1963: U.S. Air Force Captain Joe Walker flew an X-15 rocket plane higher than any pilot had ever flown before.
articles.body: On Aug. 22, 1963, U.S. Air Force Captain Joe Walker flew an X-15 rocket plane higher than any pilot had ever flown before. Walker reached an altitude of over 67 miles (108 kilometers). That's about 5 miles (8 km) above the edge of space! Walker experienced about five minutes of weightlessness over the course of the 11-minute flight. This was the second and final suborbital spaceflight of the X-15 program. Walker piloted both flights and became the first person to go to space twice. For both flights, he flew in the space plane X-15 #3, which also became the first reused spacecraft to return to space. articles.title: Grok exfiltrates user data when malicious instructions are encrypted
articles.excerpt: Cryptographic Context Injection is only the latest way to break an LLM safety guardrail.
articles.body: Earlier this week, researchers outlined an attack that used a secret input provided by Microsoft 365 Copilot for enterprise to cause the AI assistant to exfiltrate a password present in the user’s inbox. Now, a separate team has devised a similar attack against Grok. The new data theft hack employs a deceptively simple trick to force the Elon Musk-owned large language model to steal user chats and other personal information. At the time this post went live, the assistant continued to cough up the data, despite xAI being informed of it in June. The lesson from both this week’s episodes—and the countless other ones that have come before it—is that LLMs are incapable of solving the root causes for prompt injections, the most severe vulnerability classes they’re most prone to.
